title: Active learning in pre-service science teacher education
extended_summary:
This paper examines how a pre-service teacher education course can promote active learning in physics laboratory instruction. The authors focus on whether engaging teachers in inquiry-like laboratory work, collaborative group problem solving, and metacognitive reflection helps them understand active learning and transfer it into future teaching practice.

The intervention was a 30-hour course, "Physics Lab Didactics," delivered within Italy’s Formative Active Training (TFA) teacher-qualification program. Participants were pre-service teachers in two groups: Math & Science teachers for lower secondary school and Math & Physics teachers for upper secondary school, all at the University of Siena/Tuscany training sites. The course included explicit discussion of laboratory organization, safety, measurement, uncertainty, friction, observation, and other physics lab activities, with participants working in small groups and producing lab reports and proposals for active learning.

The study compares outcomes between the Siena cohort that received the active-learning-oriented physics lab course and a Pisa cohort used as a control group because it did not receive the same active learning emphasis. Preliminary results suggest the intervention was more effective for Math & Science teachers in lower secondary education than for Math & Physics teachers in upper secondary education. The authors conclude that active learning experiences combined with reflection can improve awareness and later classroom use, but that participants with stronger disciplinary focus may need a different course organization to better recognize and apply active learning.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/preliminary comparative report in teacher education, not a randomized or well-controlled causal study of AI tools. It provides descriptive evidence with a quasi-comparison group but lacks formal causal identification, effect sizes, and standardized outcomes.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests modest positive influence on teacher learning and institutional training design, but the effects are preliminary, non-quantified, and not in the target K-12 science AI domain. After retaining only true target-domain studies, the broader optimistic thesis is not supported by this paper; at most, it weakly supports the narrower claim that well-scaffolded, active-learning lab preparation can improve some pre-service teachers' understanding and classroom transfer under supervised training conditions.

finding.finding_summary: This paper evaluates a pre-service teacher education course built around active learning and inquiry-based physics laboratory work, not a K-12 AI intervention. The main reported outcome is teachers' understanding and use of active learning: preliminary assessment suggests the learning path was more effective for Math & Science teachers than for Math & Physics teachers, with some first-grade secondary teachers later transferring active learning into school training, while others remained focused on disciplinary details.
finding.measure: Lab reports, interviews on lab reports, final training reports, and oral examination performance focused on active learning understanding and application
finding.study_size: n=45 in Siena for the active-learning course (34 Math & Science, 11 Math & Physics); control group n=26 from Pisa for final reports

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that active-learning-based pre-service training and stronger school supervision can improve teacher preparation and qualification processes. It reports preliminary evidence that the redesigned course supported some participants in transferring active learning into training-at-school practice, but it also notes implementation limits and suggests the need for a different organization of TFA courses for secondary school of second grade teachers.
finding.measure: Course assessments, final reports, oral exam outcomes, and observed transfer into training-at-school practice
finding.study_size: n=45 in Siena; comparison materials from n=26 Pisa participants
